rv.q: A great part of what gives Archduke its considerable theatrical oomph is, while heading straight for the tragedy, just how funny it is.

Page is so convincing, and the staging of his soon-to-be accomplices with their backs to us, completely anonymized, so ingenuous, that “Archduke” briefly reaches a dizzying marriage of form and content.
Archduke is a bizarre Beckett-like farce with the clowns crying in the darkness, howling against the tides of history.
In any case, a visit to Joseph's capacious imagination is well worth it.
Joseph’s confused and ineffectual aspiring assassins stumble into the history books almost against their will, making Archduke sharply funny and deeply tragic.
Despite the credentials of a Tony Award-winning director and talented cast, Joseph’s Archduke falls flat when its premise is poked.

Archduke is a why of a play; still, there are good scenes, and Linda Cho's costumes, Matthew Richards' lighting, and Jane Shaw's elaborate sound design–dogs barking, thunder, foghorns, train clickety-clacks–are all first-class.
This fitfully entertaining New York premiere production of Archduke reveals it to be slight, good-natured, and ultimately unsatisfying.
Archduke never quite reaches those gasping, wheezing heights of hilarity, settling into a gentle absurdity

This proud regicide, Dragutin Dimitrijevic, a real-life figure in Balkans history, burns at the center of Archduke , an interesting, nicely written, yet not especially satisfying new drama from Rajiv Joseph.
Director Darko Tresnjak has not found the right vibe in order to make this a farce or an historical recreation.
And, despite a stellar cast including Patrick Page and Kristine Nielsen, the production is not even all that funny.

It’s no ordinary cue for intermission: the explosive word slices the air with a bracing shiver before blackout. It also neatly sums up the play’s first half, which is, quite simply, a banger. The second act may not fully sustain that momentum, but taken as a whole, this darkly comic drama is very much a coup.
Archduke gets at the pathetic underpinnings of our current situation without nudging the audience too roughly.
Given its grave subject matter, the surprise of Archduke is its entertainment value.
Archduke is a diverting bit of alternate history, with some fine comic moments and an underlying message about how easy it can be to radicalize youth.
Page, maximizing his signature basso profondo, finds an unnerving warmth in one of the key strategists behind Ferdinand's murder.
Joseph’s work is thought-provoking with a bit of humor, much of it from Nielsen.

cn.t: Joseph's dark comedy about Franz Ferdinand's assassination draws praise for Patrick Page's commanding performance and offbeat humor, though critics split on whether its tonal whiplash and historical irreverence ultimately hit or miss the mark.

vr.q: I thought the writing was sharp and the performances were great.
I really enjoyed this play. If it sounds interesting to you, please check it out.
